name: Animal Policy International: welfare standards for imported animal products (charityevals, 2025)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: a net harm at the defaults, so by where its result falls: the compliance costs of the import rules on shoppers, by branch (EU 51%, UK 39%, New Zealand 10%); the EU's part spread over its five most populous members by population, a stand-in for the whole union. The animals spared are abroad (mostly in Ukraine and Türkiye for the EU branch).
summary: Animal Policy International, founded in 2023 through Ambitious Impact's incubation programme, researches and campaigns for rules that imported eggs and pork meet the welfare standards of the country importing them, in the EU, the UK and New Zealand. No such rule has been won yet, so this model counts what its 2025 work (a declared budget of €120,000 for its EU entity, about {{row:cost_total}} for the whole organisation by our judgment) adds to the chance of three: cage-free requirements for the EU's egg imports ({{row:eu_p_adopted}} chance; about 9.3 million caged hens abroad supply them), a UK requirement on pork from sow stalls and New Zealand's bans on sow stalls and battery cages applied to imports, each at API's share of the advocates and 2025's share of its work. The hens and sows spared are counted in the shared suffering figures, and the dearer eggs and pork as a compliance cost. At the site's default weight of a chicken's pain against a person's, the shoppers' cost (for the EU, API's own estimate of the rise in egg prices, on the value of EU egg production) outweighs the hens' and sows' gain, so the result is a net harm, about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000; it turns positive only with chickens weighed about two hundred times higher. Both sides are mostly the EU branch and mostly judgment: the chance the EU rule passes, how many hens actually leave cages rather than the trade shifting, and API's small part in a crowded EU field; every branch is discounted for missing data, and the next dollar counts at {{row:marginal_vs_past_average}} of the average.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

sections.title: In chicken pain days
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for every animal model. The shared SAD figures are Ambitious Impact's, which count each species' pain as a share of a person's with its own species weights. Here those weights come out and Rethink Priorities' go in, so every species is counted in days of a chicken's disabling pain. How a chicken compares with a person is the one animal slider.

source.title: EA Funds, Animal Welfare Fund grants, January to March 2025
source.quote: Animal Policy International (55,000 EUR) This grant was co-funded with AWF.

rows.explainer: Our judgment. The declaration's one named contribution, €110,000 from Effective Ventures Foundation, is about the Animal Welfare Fund's $57,700 grant plus the €55,000 grant it co-funded (both on the Fund's January to March 2025 page), so the money routed through the Fund is inside it; what may lie outside is money the New Zealand trust (registered May 2025) and the US fiscal sponsor received. With nine staff named on its team page, some of them part time, spending a little above the declared budget is likely: 1.3, from 1 (the declaration is everything) to 2.

Cost of the modelled programmes, including overhead
EU: caged hens abroad whose eggs and egg products the EU imported in 2025

source.title: Animal Policy International, Closing the Welfare Gap on Imported Eggs (October 2026)
source.page: The effect of limiting the requirement to shell eggs
source.quote: Of the estimated 9.3 million caged hens whose products were imported into the EU in 2025, 2.3 million had their products imported in the form of dried or liquid eggs.

rows.explainer: API's own estimate from EU trade data and the production systems of the exporting countries (Ukraine, Türkiye, North Macedonia, Argentina and China, over 95% of the caged-hen imports): about 90% of EU egg imports, which are about 3% of the EU's egg use. A count of hens, not hen-years (next row). Range ours, ±25%: API's conversion of trade data through production systems and laying rates, not independently checked.

rows.label: EU: hen-years per hen (laying life)
rows.explainer: API turns the laying-hen years behind a year's imports into hens by the average laying life; a commercial hen lays for about 55 to 70 weeks. 1.15 hen-years per hen, from 1 to 1.4.

rows.label: UK: pigs a year behind the UK's pork imports (2024)

source.title: Animal Policy International with Compassion in World Farming and the RSPCA, Closing the Welfare Gap (UK, April 2025)
source.quote: The total pork imports added up to 613,957 tonnes in 2024. The imported tonnage equates to approximately 6.4 million pigs every year.

rows.explainer: API's conversion of HMRC's import tonnage; the main exporters are the Netherlands, Denmark, Germany, Ireland, France and Belgium. Range ours, ±15% (carcass weights differ by exporter).

rows.label: New Zealand: pigs a year behind its pork imports (2022)

source.title: Animal Policy International, Closing the Welfare Gap (New Zealand, 2024)
source.quote: The total pork imports added up to 50,283 tonnes in 2022 (latest figures), representing around half of total pork consumption. The imported tonnage equates to approximately 540,000 pigs every year.

rows.explainer: API's conversion; the main exporters are Spain, Germany, Poland, Canada, Finland and the US. Imports have since grown to about 60% of the pork eaten (API's 2026 figure), so this undercounts a little: range ours, 470,000 to 700,000.

rows.label: New Zealand: layer hens a year behind its egg imports (2022)

source.title: Animal Policy International, Closing the Welfare Gap (New Zealand, 2024)
source.quote: The imported tonnage equates to approximately 325,000 layer hens affected every year.

rows.explainer: API's conversion: 65% of the imports egg powder mainly from Italy, 19% liquid egg mainly from China and Australia, 16% shell eggs mainly from China. Range ours, about ±25%.

rows.label: Pigs sold per breeding sow a year (European and North American herds)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: herds in the EU and North America sell roughly 25 to 33 pigs per sow a year (Denmark and the Netherlands at the top, Poland and Spain lower). 26, from 22 to 32. Turns the pigs behind imports into the sows that bore them.

rows.label: UK: breeding sows behind the pork imports
New Zealand: breeding sows behind the pork imports
Animals a year behind the imports the branches cover
rows.explainer: For reading only: the EU's caged hens, the sows behind UK and New Zealand pork imports and New Zealand's imported hens.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for how long a won law counts before it would have come anyway (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: SADs averted per hen-year moved from a battery cage to an aviary
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: sad_factors). Most hens behind EU imports are in conventional cages; an EU requirement equivalent to the cage phase-out the Commission is preparing would need cage-free eggs.

rows.label: SADs averted per sow-year in group housing instead of gestation crates
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: sad_factors): a sow kept in groups through pregnancy, confined only around farrowing.

rows.label: EU: chance the EU adopts cage-free requirements for imported eggs
rows.explainer: The Commission's February 2025 Vision for Agriculture and Food committed it to equivalent standards for imports, particularly on animal welfare; its proposal on laying hens is due by December 2026, and a leaked draft (Agra Facts, 6 November 2026, as API reports it in its 10 November 2026 news item) includes a cage phase-out with equivalent requirements for imports. Parliament and the Council must still pass it, against trade partners' objections and some member states' doubts on cages. One chance. Our judgment: 40%, from 15% to 65%, that a requirement covering most imported eggs passes.

rows.label: EU: years from 2025 until the requirement applies
rows.explainer: Our judgment: a proposal at the end of 2026, adoption in about two years, then a transition to match the phase-out of cages in the EU itself (earlier cage bans gave producers 10 to 12 years; a short transition is more likely for imports). 8 years from mid-2025, from 5 to 12.

rows.label: EU: discounted years counted
EU: share of the hens behind imports that leave cages, rather than the trade shifting

source.title: Animal Policy International, Closing the Welfare Gap & Third Countries (November 2026)

rows.explainer: Our judgment. Exporters can meet the requirement by converting flocks, or by sending the EU eggs from cage-free farms they already have and their caged eggs elsewhere, while EU producers take back part of the market; then fewer hens leave cages than supply the EU. By API's analysis, four fifths of the imports by value come from countries that are candidates to join the EU and must align with its rules anyway, and for the others less than 5% of their cage-free production would cover their 2025 exports, so either path is cheap. 40%, from 15% to 70%. The shared leakage figure (eggs still sold elsewhere through the price response) is a side effect below, a different step.

rows.label: EU: share of the caged hens behind imports still in battery cages when the rule applies

source.title: Animal Policy International, Closing the Welfare Gap on Imported Eggs (October 2026)

rows.explainer: Our judgment. The main exporters keep most hens in conventional (battery) cages today; Ukraine and North Macedonia, candidates to join the EU, are expected to move to the EU's own enriched-cage standard before the rule applies, about eight years from 2025. 50%, from 20% to 90%; the rest are in enriched cages.

rows.label: EU: SADs averted, hens out of battery cages, discounted (before adjustments; 2024 SAD figures)
rows.formula: eu_caged_hens * eu_hen_years_per_hen * eu_conversion_share * eu_battery_share * sads_per_hen_year * eu_p_adopted * eu_discounted_years
rows.explainer: Caged hens × hen-years per hen × the share that leave cages × the battery share × SADs per hen-year (battery cage to aviary) × the chance × the discounted years counted.

rows.label: SADs averted per hen-year moved from an enriched cage to an aviary (2025 SAD figures)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: sad_factors), a 2025 SAD figure, so its SADs take the 2025 hen weight in the species step.

rows.label: EU: SADs averted, hens out of enriched cages, discounted (before adjustments; 2025 SAD figures)
rows.formula: eu_caged_hens * eu_hen_years_per_hen * eu_conversion_share * (1 - eu_battery_share) * sads_per_hen_year_enriched * eu_p_adopted * eu_discounted_years
rows.explainer: The same for the hens in enriched cages, at the enriched-cage-to-aviary figure.

rows.label: EU: SADs averted if the requirement passes, discounted (before adjustments)
UK: chance the UK requires imported pork to meet its sow-stall ban
rows.explainer: The government's 2025 Trade Strategy only commits to consider whether overseas produce has an unfair advantage, and its December 2025 Animal Welfare Strategy has no import rule; in the January 2026 Commons debate the minister made no new commitment. The cross-party Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee recommended in February 2026 that the UK seek exemptions from dynamic alignment with the EU on animal welfare, which would keep the power to set such rules. One chance. Our judgment: 8%, from 2% to 20%, that a welfare-based requirement on pork imports comes within the next several years.

rows.label: UK: share of a sow-year in stalls that a UK standard would end, across the exporters

source.title: Animal Policy International with Compassion in World Farming and the RSPCA, Closing the Welfare Gap (UK, April 2025)
source.quote: Over 50% of the pork imported into the UK is from countries that still allow the use of sow stalls, a practice banned in the UK since the 90s.

rows.explainer: Our judgment. The main exporters are EU states, where stalls are allowed only for the first four weeks of pregnancy (about a quarter of gestation; a year includes two to two and a half pregnancies), while the shared SADs figure is for a sow crated through gestation; some imports come from countries without the limit. 25% of that change, from 15% to 40%.

rows.label: UK: years from 2025 until a requirement applies, if it comes
rows.explainer: Our judgment: legislation and a transition for exporters. 4 years, from 2 to 8.

rows.label: UK: discounted years counted
UK: SADs averted if the requirement comes, discounted (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Sows behind UK pork imports × the share of the stall change × SADs per sow-year × the chance × the discounted years counted. UK egg imports are not counted: the UK still allows enriched cages, most imported egg comes from EU enriched or cage-free flocks, and battery-cage imports (from Ukraine) are a small share. Nor are fur and foie gras, which API's UK report also names: no UK proposal on them is in play, and the site has no SADs figure for fur-farmed animals or force-fed ducks.

rows.label: New Zealand: chance New Zealand applies its sow-stall and battery-cage bans to imports
rows.explainer: The government opposes it: the minister said in March 2026 that it would invite retaliation against New Zealand's exporters, and in June 2026 the select committee that heard the petition declined to back it. The Green member's bill (the Animal Products (Closing the Welfare Gap) Amendment Bill) is in the ballot and has not been drawn. The general election of 7 November 2026 could change the government. One chance. Our judgment: 4%, from 1% to 12%.

rows.label: New Zealand: years from 2025 until a requirement applies, if it comes
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the bill would require regulations for pork and eggs within two years of it taking effect, after a change of government and the bill's passage. 5 years, from 3 to 9.

rows.label: New Zealand: discounted years counted
New Zealand: share of a sow-year in stalls that its standard would end, across the exporters

source.title: Animal Policy International, Closing the Welfare Gap (New Zealand, 2024)
source.quote: (US, Germany, Poland, Spain, and Australia) all confine sows in stalls.

rows.explainer: Our judgment: the EU exporters (Spain, Germany, Poland, Finland) allow stalls for the first four weeks of pregnancy, Canada and the US through gestation in many herds; New Zealand banned stalls in 2016. 40%, from 20% to 70%, of the shared crated-to-group-housing change.

rows.label: New Zealand: share of the hens behind its egg imports that are in battery cages

source.title: Animal Policy International, Closing the Welfare Gap (New Zealand, 2024)
source.quote: come in as egg powder, primarily from Italy, 19% as liquid eggs, mainly from China and Australia, and 16% as shell eggs, mainly from China.

rows.explainer: Our judgment. By weight, 35% of the imports are liquid and shell eggs from China and Australia, mostly from battery cages, which New Zealand banned in 2023; but egg powder (65%, from Italy's EU enriched or cage-free flocks, which New Zealand's colony cages match) takes several times the hens per tonne (in API's EU data, egg products are 13% of the mass and 24% of the hens), so by hens the battery share is lower: 15%, from 8% to 35%.

rows.label: New Zealand: a move from battery to colony cages, as a share of the battery-to-aviary gain
rows.explainer: New Zealand's standard is colony (enriched) cages, not cage-free. The shared figures put an enriched-cage hen's gain from an aviary at about a sixth of a battery-caged hen's (3.05 against 17.49 SADs, on different SAD versions), so most of the gain is the move out of battery cages: 75%, from 50% to 90%.

rows.label: New Zealand: a move from battery to colony cages, as a share of the battery-to-cage-free production cost

source.title: Animal Policy International, The Cost of Cage-Free Egg Imports (November 2026)
source.quote: Van Horne and Bondt (2023) estimate that production costs in barn or aviary systems are 15% higher than in enriched cages and 21% higher than in barren battery cages.

rows.explainer: From the same production costs: battery to enriched is (1/1.15 − 1/1.21) of a barn hen's cost against (1 − 1/1.21) for battery to barn, about a quarter. 25%, from 15% to 40%.

rows.label: New Zealand: SADs averted if the requirement comes, discounted (before adjustments)
rows.formula: (nz_sows * nz_stall_gap_share * sads_per_sow_year + nz_hens * nz_battery_share * nz_colony_gain_share * sads_per_hen_year) * nz_p_adopted * nz_discounted_years
rows.explainer: (Sows × the stall change × SADs per sow-year + hens × the battery share × the colony gain × SADs per hen-year) × the chance × the discounted years counted. Fish are not counted: the proposed policy covers only pork and eggs.

rows.label: All branches: SADs averted before adjustments
SADs per animal-year (outcome-weighted, for reading only)
rows.formula: (eu_caged_hens * eu_hen_years_per_hen * (eu_battery_share * sads_per_hen_year + (1 - eu_battery_share) * sads_per_hen_year_enriched) + uk_sows * uk_stall_gap_share * sads_per_sow_year + nz_sows * nz_stall_gap_share * sads_per_sow_year + nz_hens * nz_battery_share * nz_colony_gain_share * sads_per_hen_year) / animals_per_year

rows.label: Years until effect (outcome-weighted, for reading only)
rows.formula: (eu_raw * eu_years_until_effect + uk_raw * uk_years_until_effect + nz_raw * nz_years_until_effect) / raw_total

rows.label: Discount for the wait (outcome-weighted, for reading only)
rows.explainer: Each branch's wait, discounted at the shared rate, weighted by the branches.

rows.label: Discounted years counted (outcome-weighted, for reading only)
rows.formula: (eu_raw * eu_discounted_years + uk_raw * uk_discounted_years + nz_raw * nz_discounted_years) / raw_total

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with resources others commit only because of it
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): here the governments that adopt and enforce the rules and the exporters that comply. The charity is credited this share of the good done; the rest stays with those who carry out the result.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 1: the effect is the shared SADs per change, and the uncertainty in API's animal counts is in their own ranges; that no outcome is measured is the missing-data step.

rows.label: Counterfactual adjustment
rows.explainer: 1: whether a requirement would have come anyway is the years a win counts and each branch's chance; one question (Convention 5).

rows.label: EU: API's share among those pressing for import requirements
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The Commission's commitment (February 2025) came before API's EU work; Eurogroup for Animals and its members, Compassion in World Farming, the consumer group BEUC and the farm lobby Copa-Cogeca press for the same, and the consultation drew over 230,000 replies. API is one of few groups making the trade evidence case on eggs, especially egg products. 2%, from 0.5% to 6%.

rows.label: EU: 2025's share of API's part
rows.explainer: Our judgment: in 2025 API submitted evidence to the Commission's call (July) and registered as an EU lobbyist (September); its egg-import reports came in October and November 2026 and the legislative fight is ahead. 25%, from 10% to 50%.

rows.label: EU: attribution share
rows.explainer: The share among those who pressed for it, times 2025's share of that work, times the mobiliser's share (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: UK: API's share among those pressing for import standards
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the RSPCA, Compassion in World Farming (co-publishers of API's report), the National Farmers' Union, FOUR PAWS, Humane World for Animals and Wildlife and Countryside Link press for the same; API wrote the first analysis of the UK's imports and supported the January 2026 debate, and the committee cited its evidence among six groups'. 8%, from 3% to 20%.

rows.label: UK: 2025's share of API's part
rows.explainer: Our judgment: 2025 brought the report and its parliamentary launch; the debate and committee evidence came in early 2026 and more work would be needed. 40%, from 20% to 60%.

rows.label: UK: attribution share
rows.explainer: The share among those who pressed for it, times 2025's share, times the mobiliser's share (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: New Zealand: API's share among those pressing for import standards
rows.explainer: Our judgment: API leads the campaign (reports, legal opinions, the 11,000-signature petition, the farmers' alliance), beside the SPCA, SAFE, New Zealand Pork (which has called for it since 2023) and the Green Party, which wrote the bill. 35%, from 15% to 60%.

rows.label: New Zealand: 2025's share of API's part
rows.explainer: Our judgment: 2025 brought the petition, the bill's launch and the Vision Into Action report; work since 2023 and still to come counts too. 35%, from 20% to 50%.

rows.label: New Zealand: attribution share
rows.explainer: The share among those who pressed for it, times 2025's share, times the mobiliser's share (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Enforcement: share of the covered imports that meet the requirement in practice
rows.explainer: Our judgment: these are border rules, enforced through certification and inspection, as the EU has applied its slaughter rules to imported meat since 2013; certificates can be gamed and inspection of farms abroad is thin. 85%, from 60% to 100%.

rows.label: Pledges kept
rows.explainer: 1: no company pledges are counted, so the shared rate of pledges kept (@sad_factors.commitment_fulfilment_cage_free) doesn't apply; how far the border rules are enforced is the enforcement row.

rows.label: Missing-data discount
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12) in every branch: no rule is won yet, and no study measures what import standards do to animals abroad.

rows.label: EU: adjustments multiplied
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * eu_attribution_share * implementation_adj * border_enforcement_adj * missing_data_adj

rows.label: UK: adjustments multiplied
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * uk_attribution_share * implementation_adj * border_enforcement_adj * missing_data_adj

rows.label: New Zealand: adjustments multiplied
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * nz_attribution_share * implementation_adj * border_enforcement_adj * missing_data_adj

rows.label: Share among co-advocates (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (eu_raw * eu_attribution_share_shared + uk_raw * uk_attribution_share_shared + nz_raw * nz_attribution_share_shared) / raw_total

rows.label: Attribution share (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (eu_raw * eu_attribution_share + uk_raw * uk_attribution_share + nz_raw * nz_attribution_share) / raw_total
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches' used shares, for reading only: each branch applies its own.

rows.label: All adjustments (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (eu_raw * eu_total_adj + uk_raw * uk_total_adj + nz_raw * nz_total_adj) / raw_total

rows.label: Side effect: caged eggs and crated pork still sold elsewhere, as a share of the animals' gain
rows.explainer: The shared figure: when a market stops taking caged eggs or crated pork, some is still produced and sold elsewhere through the price response (about 9% for eggs). A harm, so negative.

rows.label: Effects not modelled, as a share of the result
rows.explainer: The leakage above. Not counted: precedent for other countries and products (fish, broilers), which API argues for but no evidence sizes; any trade retaliation.

rows.label: EU: SADs averted, credited
UK: SADs averted, credited
New Zealand: SADs averted, credited
SADs averted
SADs averted per dollar of the charity's cost
Spending per person of the people who pay (rich-country stand-in, survey scale)
rows.explainer: The site's European figure (UK household consumption per person on the survey scale), standing in for the EU's, the UK's and New Zealand's shoppers.

rows.label: EU: cost a year if every caged hen behind the imports went cage-free (US dollars)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: compliance_costs): API's estimate of the rise in EU egg prices on the value of EU egg production, at producer prices (the retail margin on it is a transfer), at its enriched-cage cost gap; scaled up for the battery-caged share, whose move costs more (next row).

rows.label: EU: cost of moving a battery-caged hen over an enriched-caged one

source.title: Animal Policy International, The Cost of Cage-Free Egg Imports (November 2026)
source.quote: Van Horne and Bondt (2023) estimate that production costs in barn or aviary systems are 15% higher than in enriched cages and 21% higher than in barren battery cages.

rows.explainer: 21% over 15%: API's central estimate uses the enriched-cage gap. The two gaps are on different bases (a battery-caged hen costs less to keep); as shares of a barn hen's cost the ratio is about 1.3.

rows.label: EU: real cost of the trade that shifts, as a share of converting it

source.title: Animal Policy International, The Cost of Cage-Free Egg Imports (November 2026)
source.quote: The actual effect could be lower if exporters absorb some additional costs to remain competitive, or EU buyers shift purchases to suppliers already operating cage-free systems

rows.explainer: Our judgment. Where the trade shifts (eggs from cage-free farms that already exist sent to the EU, caged eggs sold elsewhere), the premium EU buyers pay is mostly a transfer to producers who already bear the cost, not a new cost (normalization.md 2.21 counts costs without transfers); the real cost is where dearer EU-produced eggs replace imports. 25%, from 0 (pure reshuffling) to 50%.

rows.label: EU: share of the full conversion cost that is a real cost
rows.explainer: The hens that leave cages carry their full cost; the shifted trade its real part only. So the cost matches the hens counted.

rows.label: EU: compliance cost a year (US dollars)
Cost a year of moving one battery-caged hen to cage-free (US dollars)
rows.explainer: The EU estimate at the battery-cage gap, per hen-year behind the imports.

rows.label: Compliance cost per sow-year moved from crates to group housing (US dollars, 2024 prices)
rows.explainer: The regulator's net cost of California's Proposition 12 (shared), its pork part, over the sows that supply California (shared), in 2024 dollars: the site's one figure for what a crate-free sow costs.

rows.explainer: A won rule's compliance cost (docs/normalization.md 2.21): the real cost above, valued as money lost by those who bear it (the shared payer multiple times spending per person), on the log scale; over the same chance, years, credit, enforcement and missing-data step as the hens' gain.

rows.label: UK: compliance cost, units of value (negative)
rows.formula: -uk_sows * uk_stall_gap_share * sow_cost_usd * $uov_per_ln_consumption / (@public_funds.compliance_cost_payer_multiple * payer_consumption) * uk_p_adopted * uk_discounted_years * counterfactual_adj * uk_attribution_share * border_enforcement_adj * missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The sows' change at the shared cost per crate-free sow, valued as for the EU.

rows.label: New Zealand: compliance cost, units of value (negative)
rows.formula: -(nz_sows * nz_stall_gap_share * sow_cost_usd + nz_hens * nz_battery_share * nz_colony_cost_share * eu_cost_per_battery_hen_usd) * $uov_per_ln_consumption / (@public_funds.compliance_cost_payer_multiple * payer_consumption) * nz_p_adopted * nz_discounted_years * counterfactual_adj * nz_attribution_share * border_enforcement_adj * missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The sows at the shared cost per crate-free sow; the hens at the EU estimate's cost per battery-caged hen, scaled by the colony share of the cost; valued as for the EU.
